questions.rationale: Cloned slot settings leave content absent; Standard supports live staging slots.
Fault domains address shared power and switches; update domains concern maintenance.
The sixth VM wraps to the first of five update domains; the seventh wraps to the second.
Only one update domain restarts at once, with 30-minute recovery; numerical order and application-failure protection are not promised.
Availability-set fault/update domain counts cannot change after creation; up to 20 update domains are supported.
Of Free, Basic and Standard, only Standard supports multiple deployment slots.
Swapping the same unchanged pair back restores the old production app now held in staging; cloning settings cannot restore code.
A minimum of one or more expresses an always-running replica floor; maximum alone cannot prevent zero replicas.
Independent scaling triggers use any-rule conditions rather than requiring every rule simultaneously.
Scale-rule edits create immutable revisions; replicas are instances of revisions.
Priority 200 denies before priority 300 and stops processing under the stated absence of security admin overrides.
Established SSH retains flow state after allow removal, while new connections use updated denial rules.
Allowed outbound flows receive stateful response handling without a separate inbound response rule; inbound filtering still exists.
Default NSG rules remain undeletable and are overridden through higher-priority custom rules.
Direct peering traffic uses Microsoft's backbone without requiring internet transit or a gateway.
Peering address-space changes require synchronization, rather than workload deletion or assumed automatic propagation.
Remote-gateway use excludes a local gateway; both regional and global peering support transit.
Pending private endpoints await owner approval; only Approved connections carry service traffic.
Private endpoint and VNet share subscription/region; the target resource may reside elsewhere.
ASGs group VM networking by application without explicit-address upkeep; service tags identify Azure service prefixes.
DNS hosting/API management do not purchase domain ownership; registration remains a registrar responsibility.
The parent NS delegation must use this zone's assigned Azure servers; private links and an A record named NS do not delegate publicly.
A below-apex CNAME maps a DNS name to another name; A maps IPv4 and MX identifies mail exchange.
Two api IPv4 values belong to one A record set; duplicate name/type record sets and IP-valued CNAMEs are invalid.
TTL determines cache lifetime; changing authoritative TTL does not purge previously cached answers or alter TCP timeouts.
Resolution-only private-zone links permit manual and autoregistered record lookup but do not automatically register new VM records.
A VNet has one autoregistration zone but may have multiple resolution zones; a zone may have multiple registering VNets.
Private DNS supplies managed internal names and optional VM autoregistration, without public registrar service or internet delegation.
A Layer-4 TCP workload behind one frontend fits Load Balancer; NSGs filter and DNS record sets do not supply backend probes.
Internal Load Balancer uses a private frontend, consistent with the case's private TCP API; public frontend/DNS-only designs fail this requirement.
A backend pool identifies VM targets and a rule maps frontend 443 to backend 8443; NSG priority and MX records are unrelated.
An HTTP probe treats 503 as unhealthy and excludes that backend from new flows; the case and exhibit are consistent.
A TCP handshake checks listener reachability rather than HTTP response semantics or every dependency.
NSG and guest-firewall probe-port/source permissions can independently block the listener; DNS TTL and deleting backends do not repair filtering.
IPv4 platform probes originate from 168.63.129.16, identified by AzureLoadBalancer, rather than frontend or workstation IP.
One failed probe excludes its backend from new connections while healthy backends remain eligible; probes do not guarantee resets or repair apps.
Zone creation precedes obtaining its assigned servers, parent delegation, and cache-aware recursive verification; the ordered key reflects dependencies.
TCP establishes a connection; HTTP requires 200 without TLS; HTTPS adds TLS and still requires 200. Match prompts and ordered answer mapping agree.
A, AAAA and MX map respectively to IPv4, IPv6 and mail-exchanger preference; all match prompts agree with the ordered key.
Chosen addressing/probe values precede component creation, then the referencing load-balancing rule, then end-to-end verification.
A /29 has eight IPv4 addresses and Azure reserves five, leaving exactly three usable addresses.
10.40.2.0/24 falls outside the sole 10.40.0.0/24 VNet range; additional containing address space is needed, not NSG/public-IP changes.
10.50.1.128/25 lies inside 10.50.1.0/24; overlap violates subnet requirements, while multiple subnets and unequal lengths are allowed.
10.0.8.0/24 overlaps 10.0.0.0/16 and prevents peering; unequal prefix lengths themselves are valid.
The diagram's A-B-C peerings provide no transitive A-C path under the explicit absence of gateways and forwarding.
Hub allow-gateway-transit and spoke use-remote-gateways settings supply explicit transit; a spoke cannot retain its own gateway.
New peered ranges require synchronization and nonoverlap checking; private DNS links or VM deletion do not advertise ranges.
Standard public IPv4 allocation is static; Basic dynamic behavior and private DHCP are unrelated.
Current Microsoft public-IP documentation records Basic retirement on September 30, 2025; Standard remains supported in October 2026.
Standard VM public-IP inbound access requires an applicable permitting NSG; address assignment supplies neither universal allowance nor payload encryption.
For 10.80.4.19, /24 is the longest matching prefix and selects appliance-B; no packet duplication follows.
For identical valid prefixes, UDR outranks BGP under the expressly excluded special service-endpoint case; NSG numbers do not choose routes.
The workload subnet needs its route-table association and Virtual appliance next hop with the appliance private IP; DNS/ASG objects are not next hops.
A selected None next hop drops packets, rather than queuing them or routing to the internet.
Connection troubleshoot diagnoses reachability from a VM to a specific endpoint; tags and MX records cannot test TCP connectivity.
Effective NIC routes expose combined routing and the source subnet association determines whether UDRs apply; DNS/NSG priorities cannot change either.
NSG packet attributes and matching TCP 443 allow rules govern the stated HTTPS access; they neither admit TCP 80 nor renew certificates.
All ASG member NICs must inhabit one VNet; multiple eligible NICs and private-only VMs are supported.
Both inbound subnet and NIC NSGs must permit the flow; the shown subnet deny wins regardless of the NIC allow.
Outbound NIC denial blocks before the subnet allow; separate NSGs do not delete or globally override one another.
Effective security rules aggregate applicable subnet/NIC filtering; DNS and storage keys contain no such rule view.
New dedicated Basic Bastion requires AzureBastionSubnet and /26 or larger; the scenario excludes Developer and historical /27 exceptions.
Public Basic Bastion requires an unused Standard static public IP, distinct from Developer and Premium private-only modes.
Custom Bastion ports require Standard or higher; Basic and DNS TTL cannot enable that capability.
Service endpoints extend subnet identity and route service traffic over the backbone; they neither create a private-endpoint NIC nor grant data permissions.
Subnet endpoint enablement must be paired with resource-side VNet restriction policy; enabling it alone leaves broad storage access unchanged.
On-premises VPN clients do not inherit service-endpoint subnet identity; DNS aliases and endpoint NIC assumptions cannot grant it.
Approved private endpoints use subnet private IPs and correct service-name DNS; neither client public IPs nor service-endpoint identity replaces that model.
Pending storage connections need resource-owner approval; TTL and NSG changes cannot approve them, consistent with the shared case.
Blob requires the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net endpoint record and client-VNet link; Files and MX records cannot resolve its private hostname.
The read-only nameServers resource-property reference creates an implicit Bicep dependency; independent resources can deploy in parallel.
Even cluster-supported running-VM resizing restarts the VM; failed requested-size display is not proof of successful allocation and disks are retained.
An HTTP revision's minimum of one or higher retains idle capacity; maximum-only and zero minimum do not express the requirement.
App Service private endpoints handle the missing inbound direction; existing VNet integration supplies only outbound database access.
10.42.8.19 selects the more specific /24 None route over /0 appliance route; prefix length precedes equal-prefix type precedence.
Within one NSG, priority 220 allow matches first and ends processing before 310 deny; later denial does not globally override it.
A failing Standard Load Balancer backend stops receiving new flows while other healthy backends serve; no deletion or DNS delegation occurs.
The exhibit's valid default 2 is selected when omitted; allowed value 4 is a constraint, not a default selection.
Secure decorators protect string and object parameter values; integer length and secret-prefixed naming cannot secure the credential.
The resourceGroup-scoped exhibit is deployed with az deployment group create to rg-scan; subscription deployment and group creation serve different purposes.

The scenario now explicitly specifies default Provider validation. Its keyed permissions and every explanation are consistent with that mode; the corrected explanation distinguishes ProviderNoRbac resource-read checks. Reader also lacks deployment operations under the stated no-other-assignments assumption.

resolvedFindings.claim: What-if requires deployment permissions and write access to the resources being deployed (without specifying validation mode).
resolvedFindings.rationale: Current official docs support default Provider validation and ProviderNoRbac, which checks only resource read permissions; Template skips provider permission checks. The default question should identify its mode so the explanation remains accurate. Reader insufficiency for deployment operations remains distinct from resource-write checks.

replacementProposal.scenario: An auditor has Reader on a resource group and asks to run what-if for a Bicep deployment that creates a VM, using the default Provider validation level. No other permission assignments apply.
replacementProposal.options.c.text: Default Provider what-if validation requires deployment permissions and write access to the resources being deployed
replacementProposal.options.c.explanation: With the default Provider validation level, what-if checks full deployment permissions, including resource write operations and deployment operations. ProviderNoRbac instead checks resource read permissions, so the validation mode matters.
replacementProposal.summaryExplanation: With the default Provider validation level, what-if checks full deployment permissions, including resource write operations and deployment operations. ProviderNoRbac instead checks resource read permissions, so the validation mode matters.

questions.rationale: ARM allowedValues restricts SKU choices and defaultValue supplies omitted Standard_LRS; secureString and renaming do not implement that contract.
CLI sequential evaluation means the later inline Standard_GRS overrides earlier file Standard_LRS; no concatenation occurs.
NoChange predicts unchanged redeployed properties, whereas Ignore after expansion limits indicates omitted analysis requiring investigation.
Current-resource export captures later portal tags; historical template and original parameter inputs cannot include subsequent manual edits.
The scenario expressly mandates export, JSON correction, decompile, generated-Bicep review, then what-if; source cautions support each stage.
Decompilation lacks guaranteed perfect mapping and exported schemas/password omissions require review; format conversion cannot confer approval.
The valid parameter-complete module exhibit causes webApp.bicep resources to deploy with the parent; modules are neither comments nor ignored declarations.
Parameter, variable, module and output purposes match c,d,a,b respectively; all four explanations agree with Bicep declaration semantics.
Measured memory pressure calls for adequate memory-optimized RAM; low CPU alone and disk enlargement do not solve that bottleneck.
Unavailable current-cluster target size can require deallocation and service interruption; disk capacity and tags cannot release compute placement.
Running resize restarts; managed OS/data disks survive deallocation; requested-size model display after failure does not prove allocation.
Premium SSD v2 cannot be an OS disk and lacks host caching; select an eligible OS type and reserve v2 for supported data workloads.
Ultra Disk supports performance changes without VM restart and lacks caching; it supports neither OS-disk use nor availability sets.
Historical ADE use excludes encryption at host; never-ADE VMs still require supported sizes and subscription prerequisites.
Managed-disk customer-managed keys are stored in Key Vault or Managed HSM, not tags or temporary guest disks.
A new 3-TiB Linux disk requires GPT and UUID-based persistent mounting; filesystem formatting remains necessary and fixed device IDs are unreliable.
Same-tenant cross-subscription moves require the VM and dependent disks/NIC/VNet together after validation; split-resource proposals violate dependency rules.
Zones are physically separate within a supported region with independent power/network/cooling; replicated case VMs mitigate datacenter loss, not every regional disaster.
Encryption at host covers temporary disks and OS/data caches without guest encryption/VM CPU consumption; placement and managed-disk SSE alone do not express that coverage.
Prepared Resource Mover resources enter Initiate move pending, then Commit move pending; the case explicitly validates before commit/discard decision.
Flexible orchestration manages standard VMs with individual VM/NIC/disk APIs and supported mixed types; Uniform VMSS APIs and availability sets differ.
A valid scaling profile supports metric-threshold and schedule autoscale; disk capacity and fault-domain count do not create instances on demand.
Container Registry stores images/artifacts; ACI runs containers and availability sets address VM placement.
Non-ABAC pull-only uses AcrPull; ABAC repositories use Repository Reader. AcrPush grants extra push permission and ABAC changes role applicability.
Linux containers in one ACI group share localhost ports even when not externally exposed; separate groups do not share that namespace.
ACI sums both requests: 1.5+0.5 CPUs and 2+1 GB produce 2 CPUs/3 GB, with overhead expressly excluded.
The configured two-CPU limit permits borrowing available group CPU beyond the one-CPU request; limits do not create extra hosts or capacity.
ACI defaults to Always and OnFailure retries nonzero failures; successful finite jobs stop under OnFailure, and group IP can change on restart.
Either custom-scale trigger may initiate scaling subject to replica limits; all-rule AND and disabling scaling are unsupported.
Editing scale rules creates a new revision; multiple-revision mode does not imply deleting prior revisions.
Internal app ingress scopes direct access to the same environment, with the scenario explicitly excluding environment-level route exceptions; replica count does not isolate ingress.
Always defaults to restarts, Never prevents successful-exit restart with nonzero platform-retry caveat, and OnFailure retries failures; b,c,a mapping agrees.
HTTP scale-out is bounded by maxReplicas 10; minReplicas is a floor and concurrentRequests 20 is a request threshold, not replica quantity.
HTTP ingress and multiple revision mode support immutable revision identification and traffic splitting between active revisions; replica counts and deletion claims differ.
With per-app and automatic app scaling explicitly excluded, apps share plan VMs and scale together; SQL dependencies scale separately.
Changing the pricing tier is scale up; adding VM instances is scale out and DNS cannot alter plan capacity.
CPU thresholds and business-hours schedules require Azure autoscale; App Service automatic scaling instead follows HTTP traffic.

Supported automatic backups require no initial configuration and are not downloadable; configured custom backups support on-demand/scheduled downloadable storage blobs; automatic backups omit linked databases.
Seabrook's same-region private-database outbound calls require VNet integration; app private endpoints and TLS bindings address different requirements.
The Standard app supports private endpoints, and disabling public network access removes coexisting public exposure; outbound integration and instance count do not isolate inbound access.

The SNI-capable private portal requires documented custom-hostname mapping/ownership verification and matching-certificate SNI binding; networking alone and unrelated certificates cannot satisfy HTTPS.
With ordinary apex DNS, an A record plus documented asuid TXT verification meets mapping guidance; apex CNAME and MX do not.
Restore stops the target, so restoring to a slot, validating, then swapping minimizes production interruption; cloning configuration does not restore content.
The 14-GB custom request exceeds the 10-GB total; the 4-GB database allowance is optional and automatic's 30-GB limit does not apply.
Slot-marked connection strings stick to production and custom domains do not swap; unchanged override settings preserve documented non-swapped TLS/domain behavior.
A Standard IP-based TLS binding creates a dedicated IP requiring the existing A record to be remapped; retaining shared IP or deleting hostname contradicts the documented procedure.
